title: Sliding Window Maximum
oneLinerQuestion: Find the maximum element within every sliding window of size k moving across an array.
explanation:
Problem Intuition: The Sliding Window Maximum problem requires determining the maximum value within every contiguous sliding window of size k moving across an array of length N. A brute-force approach scanning each window takes O(N * k) time, while a max-heap or balanced BST achieves O(N log k). To reach optimal O(N) linear time, we use a monotonic decreasing double-ended queue (Deque) storing array indices. By maintaining elements in strictly decreasing order of their corresponding values, the maximum element for the current window is guaranteed to reside at the front of the deque in O(1) time. As new elements enter the window, smaller elements at the back are popped because they can never be the maximum of this or any subsequent window, and indices that slide out of range are evicted from the front.

- Step 1: Data Structures Initialization — We initialize an empty double-ended queue `deque = []` (storing indices) and an array `result = []` to collect the maximum of each valid window.

- Step 2: Linear Stream Traversal — We iterate through the array using index `i` from `0` to `nums.length - 1`.

- Step 3: Evicting Out-of-Bounds Indices (Front Cleanup) — Before processing `nums[i]`, we check if the index at the front of the deque has expired: `if (deque.length > 0 && deque[0] <= i - k)`. If true, the front element falls outside the current window `[i - k + 1, i]`, so we remove it via `deque.shift()`.

- Step 4: Maintaining Monotonic Decreasing Order (Back Cleanup) — While the deque is non-empty and the value at the current index is strictly greater than the value corresponding to the tail index (`nums[i] > nums[deque[deque.length - 1]]`), we pop the tail: `deque.pop()`. Smaller preceding values are rendered obsolete because the incoming `nums[i]` is both larger and will persist longer in future windows.

- Step 5: Enqueueing Current Index — We push the current index onto the back of the deque: `deque.push(i)`.

- Step 6: Recording Window Maximum — Once the sliding window reaches full capacity (`i >= k - 1`), the index at the front of the deque (`deque[0]`) represents the maximum value for the active window. We record it: `result.push(nums[deque[0]])`.

- Step 7: Termination & Result Return — After traversing the entire array, `result` holds the maximum values for all `N - k + 1` sliding windows, which we return.

- Complexity & Memory Guarantees — Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the length of `nums`, as each index is pushed into and popped from the deque at most once across the traversal. Space Complexity: O(k) auxiliary space to maintain at most k indices inside the monotonic deque at any given moment.
pseudoCode:
FUNCTION maxSlidingWindow(nums, k):
    output = [], q = NEW Deque(), l = 0
    FOR r FROM 0 TO LENGTH(nums) - 1 DO:
        WHILE NOT IS_EMPTY(q) AND nums[LAST(q)] < nums[r] DO POP_BACK(q)
        PUSH_BACK(r) TO q
        IF l > FIRST(q) THEN POP_FRONT(q)
        IF (r + 1) >= k THEN:
            APPEND nums[FIRST(q)] TO output
            l = l + 1
        END IF
    END FOR
    RETURN output
END FUNCTION
